concepts.instructorExplanation: Run 'nft list ruleset' in the terminal and point out the packet and byte counters attached to each rule. Trigger a curl command and run the command again to show live counter updates.
knowledgeCheckObjectives: Construct nftables tables and base chains.
Analyze live counter telemetry.
concepts.diagramSpecification: Diagram of nftables kernel VM showing bytecode evaluation of match expressions and counter updates.

concepts.title: Directional Policy Management: LAN-to-WAN, LAN-to-DMZ, WAN-to-DMZ & DMZ Isolation
learningObjectives: Implement standard enterprise directional policies across all four boundary flows.
Enforce strict default-deny perimeter posture.
Configure security logging, audit alert prefixes, and establish rule hygiene best practices.
concepts.conceptIntroduction: Directional policy management brings together interface mapping, routing, 5-tuple filtering, and connection tracking into a cohesive enterprise security matrix. An enterprise firewall must define explicit rules for every directional transition between LAN, WAN, and DMZ.
concepts.purpose: Enforce business-justified network access across organizational zones while recording security audit trails and preventing unauthorized lateral traversal.
howItWorks:
1. Policy Matrix Design: Define permissions for each directional pair:
   - Flow 1 (LAN -> WAN): Outbound internet browsing (HTTP/HTTPS/DNS) with SNAT/Masquerade.
   - Flow 2 (LAN -> DMZ): Internal management and testing (HTTP/SSH) permitted.
   - Flow 3 (WAN -> DMZ): Inbound public web publishing strictly restricted to port 80/443.
   - Flow 4 (DMZ -> LAN): STRICTLY BLOCKED to prevent pivot attacks.
   - Flow 5 (DMZ -> WAN): Restricted to authorized software update repositories.
2. Default Deny: Final rule drops and logs all unmatched traffic across all boundaries.
3. Logging: Dropped packets emit structured syslog alerts with interface and IP metadata.
concepts.architectureOrWorkflow:
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       ENTERPRISE DIRECTIONAL POLICY MATRIX                    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
INGRESS ZONE  -->  EGRESS ZONE   ALLOWED SERVICES            ACTION / POSTURE
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LAN (eth1)         WAN (eth2)    HTTP, HTTPS, DNS            PERMIT & SNAT
LAN (eth1)         DMZ (eth0)    HTTP, HTTPS, SSH            PERMIT
WAN (eth2)         DMZ (eth0)    HTTP:80, HTTPS:443 only     PERMIT (Pinhole)
DMZ (eth0)         LAN (eth1)    ANY                         DENY & LOG (Isolated!)
WAN (eth2)         LAN (eth1)    ANY                         DENY & LOG (Blocked!)
ANY                ANY           ANY (Unmatched)             DEFAULT-DENY DROP
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
concepts.enterpriseExample: In the ESCI capstone topology, sxl-fw01 enforces this exact matrix: research students on the LAN can browse external web sites and manage the DMZ portal; external internet hosts can only view the DMZ website; if an attacker compromises the DMZ web server, all connection attempts toward the LAN are immediately blocked and logged.
concepts.configurationRelevance:
FortiOS Complete Policy Matrix:
config firewall policy
    edit 1
        set name "LAN-to-WAN-Internet"
        set srcintf "port2"
        set dstintf "port1"
        set action accept
        set nat enable
    next
    edit 2
        set name "LAN-to-DMZ-Admin"
        set srcintf "port2"
        set dstintf "port3"
        set action accept
    next
    edit 3
        set name "WAN-to-DMZ-Web"
        set srcintf "port1"
        set dstintf "port3"
        set service "HTTP" "HTTPS"
        set action accept
    next
    edit 4
        set name "DMZ-to-LAN-Deny"
        set srcintf "port3"
        set dstintf "port2"
        set action deny
        set logtraffic all
    next
end

Linux nftables Implementation:
nft add rule inet filter forward iifname "eth1" oifname "eth2" accept
nft add rule inet filter forward iifname "eth1" oifname "eth0" accept
nft add rule inet filter forward iifname "eth2" oifname "eth0" tcp dport { 80, 443 } accept
nft add rule inet filter forward iifname "eth0" oifname "eth1" log prefix "[DMZ-VIOLATION]: " drop
nft add rule inet filter forward log prefix "[DEFAULT-DROP]: " drop
concepts.practicalRelevance: In Day 2 Lab 3, students implement and verify all four directional policies. They run the comprehensive verification suite, confirming 100% test passing across LAN access, DMZ publishing, and DMZ isolation.
commonMistakes: Creating bidirectional permit rules when only unidirectional access is required.
Disabling logging on drop rules to save disk space.
Failing to review and decommission obsolete policies periodically.
keyTakeaways: Directional policy enforcement must govern every interface pair individually.
The default-deny posture guarantees that new unvetted services are blocked by default.
Structured security logging with unique log prefixes provides real-time visibility into policy violations.

knowledgeCheck.question: In the standard enterprise directional security matrix, what is the mandatory policy for traffic originating in the DMZ and destined for the LAN?
options: Permit with Source NAT
Deny and Log (strict isolation)
Permit only during daytime hours
Forward to external DNS servers
knowledgeCheck.explanation: DMZ servers are semi-trusted and directly exposed to the internet. Allowing them to initiate connections into the internal LAN creates an intolerable lateral movement risk.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary operational value of adding a descriptive 'log prefix' (e.g. '[DMZ-VIOLATION]: ') to drop rules?
options: It reduces log file storage size by 50%
It allows SIEM filters and SOC analysts to instantly classify, alert, and report on specific policy breaches
It speeds up packet routing
It sends an email to the client operating system
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Distinct log prefixes allow log parsers, SIEMs, and security analysts to filter and trigger high-priority alerts when forbidden inter-zone traffic is attempted.

concepts.technicalExplanation: Directional policy management coordinates stateful Netfilter inspection, zone demarcation, and logging. Explicit policy matrices ensure comprehensive coverage with zero uninspected bypass paths.
concepts.securityEngineeringRelevance: Consistent directional policy architecture prevents firewall rulebases from devolving into chaotic, unmaintainable permit lists over time.
concepts.instructorExplanation: Summarize Day 2 by showing how interface configuration (Session 2), routing (Session 3), and ACL management (Session 4) combine to form this complete, production-grade security architecture.
knowledgeCheckObjectives: Construct an enterprise directional policy matrix.
Configure audit logging prefixes for security monitoring.
concepts.diagramSpecification: Comprehensive matrix diagram showing all 4 inter-zone traffic flows and their security actions.
